weeks.title: Exercise science foundations
weeks.essentialQuestion: How can evidence, safe technique, and individual response guide decisions about exercise science foundations?
weeks.scenario: A Grade 10 learner must make a defensible decision involving exercise science foundations using limited time, ordinary resources, and a need for safe, inclusive alternatives.
weeks.model: Worked model: define the goal for exercise science foundations, identify a measurable variable, choose a safe and accessible method, collect evidence, and revise the plan when the evidence or conditions change.

days.concept: Explain the main exercise-science principle behind exercise science foundations and distinguish observation from assumption.
days.workedExample: A learner compares two approaches to exercise science foundations and identifies which claim is actually supported by the available evidence.
days.independentTask: Write a short explanation of exercise science foundations using one measurable variable and one limitation.
days.successCriteria: I can explain the principle, name useful evidence, and identify one limitation without making health diagnoses.
days.instruction: Explain the main exercise-science principle behind exercise science foundations and distinguish observation from assumption.
days.practice: Write a short explanation of exercise science foundations using one measurable variable and one limitation.
days.evidence: I can explain the principle, name useful evidence, and identify one limitation without making health diagnoses.

days.concept: Analyze technique, intensity, duration, frequency, environment, or recovery variables that can change outcomes in exercise science foundations.
days.workedExample: A learner changes one variable at a time and explains why changing several variables together would make the result harder to interpret.
days.independentTask: Choose two variables relevant to exercise science foundations and explain which should be held steady for a fair comparison.
days.successCriteria: I can identify variables, control confounders, and justify a safe technique or program choice.
days.instruction: Analyze technique, intensity, duration, frequency, environment, or recovery variables that can change outcomes in exercise science foundations.
days.practice: Choose two variables relevant to exercise science foundations and explain which should be held steady for a fair comparison.
days.evidence: I can identify variables, control confounders, and justify a safe technique or program choice.

days.concept: Apply exercise science foundations to a realistic training or recreation decision while respecting comfort, access, recovery, and stop cues.
days.workedExample: A learner selects a moderate starting option, defines a stop/adapt cue, and records how success will be evaluated.
days.independentTask: Design a brief fictional plan using exercise science foundations with a goal, starting dose, adaptation, and evidence measure.
days.successCriteria: I can create a feasible plan that includes evidence, safety, and adaptation.
days.instruction: Apply exercise science foundations to a realistic training or recreation decision while respecting comfort, access, recovery, and stop cues.
days.practice: Design a brief fictional plan using exercise science foundations with a goal, starting dose, adaptation, and evidence measure.
days.evidence: I can create a feasible plan that includes evidence, safety, and adaptation.

days.concept: Interpret a small dataset or training log related to exercise science foundations and separate a pattern from a causal claim.
days.workedExample: A learner notices improvement across several sessions but avoids claiming one variable caused the change without a comparison or controlled design.
days.independentTask: Describe one pattern, one uncertainty, and one additional observation that would strengthen an interpretation.
days.successCriteria: I can interpret data conservatively and identify uncertainty or measurement limits.
days.instruction: Interpret a small dataset or training log related to exercise science foundations and separate a pattern from a causal claim.
days.practice: Describe one pattern, one uncertainty, and one additional observation that would strengthen an interpretation.
days.evidence: I can interpret data conservatively and identify uncertainty or measurement limits.

days.concept: Defend a decision about exercise science foundations, respond to a counterexample, and revise the plan using evidence.
days.workedExample: A learner explains why a plan should change after new evidence about recovery, environment, access, or technique becomes available.
days.independentTask: Write a final claim-evidence-reasoning response and one revision condition for exercise science foundations.
days.successCriteria: I can defend a decision, respond to contrary evidence, and revise responsibly.
days.instruction: Defend a decision about exercise science foundations, respond to a counterexample, and revise the plan using evidence.
days.practice: Write a final claim-evidence-reasoning response and one revision condition for exercise science foundations.
days.evidence: I can defend a decision, respond to contrary evidence, and revise responsibly.

weeks.misconception: More intensity, more duration, or a higher number automatically proves better learning in exercise science foundations.
weeks.correction: Grade 10 PE evaluates reasoning, safe technique, evidence, program decisions, and adaptation—not body traits, comparison, or maximum effort.
weeks.teacherNotes: Require neutral language, an accessible alternative, and evidence-based reasoning for exercise science foundations. Do not require private health or body data.

Use the most difficult option because harder work always proves greater mastery.

weeks.title: Training adaptations

weeks.title: Interval training decisions

days.concept: Explain the main exercise-science principle behind interval training decisions and distinguish observation from assumption.
days.workedExample: A learner compares two approaches to interval training decisions and identifies which claim is actually supported by the available evidence.

days.concept: Analyze technique, intensity, duration, frequency, environment, or recovery variables that can change outcomes in interval training decisions.

days.successCriteria: I can identify variables, control confounders, and justify a safe technique or program choice.
days.instruction: Analyze technique, intensity, duration, frequency, environment, or recovery variables that can change outcomes in interval training decisions.

days.concept: Apply interval training decisions to a realistic training or recreation decision while respecting comfort, access, recovery, and stop cues.

weeks.title: Biomechanics of movement
weeks.essentialQuestion: How can evidence, safe technique, and individual response guide decisions about biomechanics of movement?
weeks.scenario: A Grade 10 learner must make a defensible decision involving biomechanics of movement using limited time, ordinary resources, and a need for safe, inclusive alternatives.
weeks.model: Worked model: define the goal for biomechanics of movement, identify a measurable variable, choose a safe and accessible method, collect evidence, and revise the plan when the evidence or conditions change.

days.concept: Explain the main exercise-science principle behind biomechanics of movement and distinguish observation from assumption.
days.workedExample: A learner compares two approaches to biomechanics of movement and identifies which claim is actually supported by the available evidence.
days.independentTask: Write a short explanation of biomechanics of movement using one measurable variable and one limitation.
days.successCriteria: I can explain the principle, name useful evidence, and identify one limitation without making health diagnoses.
days.instruction: Explain the main exercise-science principle behind biomechanics of movement and distinguish observation from assumption.
days.practice: Write a short explanation of biomechanics of movement using one measurable variable and one limitation.
days.evidence: I can explain the principle, name useful evidence, and identify one limitation without making health diagnoses.

days.concept: Analyze technique, intensity, duration, frequency, environment, or recovery variables that can change outcomes in biomechanics of movement.
days.workedExample: A learner changes one variable at a time and explains why changing several variables together would make the result harder to interpret.
days.independentTask: Choose two variables relevant to biomechanics of movement and explain which should be held steady for a fair comparison.
days.successCriteria: I can identify variables, control confounders, and justify a safe technique or program choice.
days.instruction: Analyze technique, intensity, duration, frequency, environment, or recovery variables that can change outcomes in biomechanics of movement.
days.practice: Choose two variables relevant to biomechanics of movement and explain which should be held steady for a fair comparison.
days.evidence: I can identify variables, control confounders, and justify a safe technique or program choice.

days.concept: Apply biomechanics of movement to a realistic training or recreation decision while respecting comfort, access, recovery, and stop cues.
days.workedExample: A learner selects a moderate starting option, defines a stop/adapt cue, and records how success will be evaluated.
days.independentTask: Design a brief fictional plan using biomechanics of movement with a goal, starting dose, adaptation, and evidence measure.
days.successCriteria: I can create a feasible plan that includes evidence, safety, and adaptation.
days.instruction: Apply biomechanics of movement to a realistic training or recreation decision while respecting comfort, access, recovery, and stop cues.
days.practice: Design a brief fictional plan using biomechanics of movement with a goal, starting dose, adaptation, and evidence measure.
days.evidence: I can create a feasible plan that includes evidence, safety, and adaptation.

days.concept: Interpret a small dataset or training log related to biomechanics of movement and separate a pattern from a causal claim.
days.workedExample: A learner notices improvement across several sessions but avoids claiming one variable caused the change without a comparison or controlled design.
days.independentTask: Describe one pattern, one uncertainty, and one additional observation that would strengthen an interpretation.
days.successCriteria: I can interpret data conservatively and identify uncertainty or measurement limits.
days.instruction: Interpret a small dataset or training log related to biomechanics of movement and separate a pattern from a causal claim.
days.practice: Describe one pattern, one uncertainty, and one additional observation that would strengthen an interpretation.

days.concept: Defend a decision about biomechanics of movement, respond to a counterexample, and revise the plan using evidence.

days.independentTask: Write a final claim-evidence-reasoning response and one revision condition for biomechanics of movement.
days.successCriteria: I can defend a decision, respond to contrary evidence, and revise responsibly.

weeks.misconception: More intensity, more duration, or a higher number automatically proves better learning in biomechanics of movement.
weeks.correction: Grade 10 PE evaluates reasoning, safe technique, evidence, program decisions, and adaptation—not body traits, comparison, or maximum effort.
weeks.teacherNotes: Require neutral language, an accessible alternative, and evidence-based reasoning for biomechanics of movement. Do not require private health or body data.

days.concept: Analyze technique, intensity, duration, frequency, environment, or recovery variables that can change outcomes in stress and recovery.

weeks.title: Accessibility and adaptations
weeks.essentialQuestion: How can evidence, safe technique, and individual response guide decisions about accessibility and adaptations?
weeks.scenario: A Grade 10 learner must make a defensible decision involving accessibility and adaptations using limited time, ordinary resources, and a need for safe, inclusive alternatives.
weeks.model: Worked model: define the goal for accessibility and adaptations, identify a measurable variable, choose a safe and accessible method, collect evidence, and revise the plan when the evidence or conditions change.

days.concept: Explain the main exercise-science principle behind accessibility and adaptations and distinguish observation from assumption.
days.workedExample: A learner compares two approaches to accessibility and adaptations and identifies which claim is actually supported by the available evidence.
days.independentTask: Write a short explanation of accessibility and adaptations using one measurable variable and one limitation.
days.successCriteria: I can explain the principle, name useful evidence, and identify one limitation without making health diagnoses.
days.instruction: Explain the main exercise-science principle behind accessibility and adaptations and distinguish observation from assumption.
days.practice: Write a short explanation of accessibility and adaptations using one measurable variable and one limitation.
days.evidence: I can explain the principle, name useful evidence, and identify one limitation without making health diagnoses.

days.concept: Analyze technique, intensity, duration, frequency, environment, or recovery variables that can change outcomes in accessibility and adaptations.
days.workedExample: A learner changes one variable at a time and explains why changing several variables together would make the result harder to interpret.
days.independentTask: Choose two variables relevant to accessibility and adaptations and explain which should be held steady for a fair comparison.
days.successCriteria: I can identify variables, control confounders, and justify a safe technique or program choice.
days.instruction: Analyze technique, intensity, duration, frequency, environment, or recovery variables that can change outcomes in accessibility and adaptations.
days.practice: Choose two variables relevant to accessibility and adaptations and explain which should be held steady for a fair comparison.
days.evidence: I can identify variables, control confounders, and justify a safe technique or program choice.

days.concept: Apply accessibility and adaptations to a realistic training or recreation decision while respecting comfort, access, recovery, and stop cues.
days.workedExample: A learner selects a moderate starting option, defines a stop/adapt cue, and records how success will be evaluated.

days.successCriteria: I can create a feasible plan that includes evidence, safety, and adaptation.
days.instruction: Apply accessibility and adaptations to a realistic training or recreation decision while respecting comfort, access, recovery, and stop cues.
days.practice: Design a brief fictional plan using accessibility and adaptations with a goal, starting dose, adaptation, and evidence measure.
days.evidence: I can create a feasible plan that includes evidence, safety, and adaptation.

days.concept: Interpret a small dataset or training log related to accessibility and adaptations and separate a pattern from a causal claim.

days.independentTask: Describe one pattern, one uncertainty, and one additional observation that would strengthen an interpretation.
days.successCriteria: I can interpret data conservatively and identify uncertainty or measurement limits.

days.concept: Defend a decision about accessibility and adaptations, respond to a counterexample, and revise the plan using evidence.
